how:77961ee1727b:fd09d9628ab5:c843a127d8.q: What does the /byok command do, and how do I use it?
how:77961ee1727b:fd09d9628ab5:c843a127d8.answer: The `/byok` command lets Freebuff CLI users route inference to their own provider (OpenRouter or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint) by referencing an environment-variable name, never pasting a key into the command. It does not enter command history, and switching sources resets the transcript. Usage: `/byok add <name> <openrouter|openai-compatible> <model> <ENV_VAR> [base-url] [--context-window=N] [--max-output-tokens=N]`, then `/byok select <name>`.

how:bc0feaf7054c:fd09d9628ab5:37fd050122.q: What does the /copy command do, and how do I use it?
how:bc0feaf7054c:fd09d9628ab5:37fd050122.answer: The /copy command exports the current conversation to your clipboard as formatted Markdown. Typing /copy (or /copy-chat) serializes your messages, the assistant's replies and reasoning, and any tool calls with their inputs and outputs into Markdown and writes it to the system clipboard, ready to paste anywhere. An /export alias also exists. For local sessions it copies the full transcript, but for remote sessions it uses OSC 52, which has a ~22 KB text budget: it first omits the largest tool results/inputs with a short note, and if that still isn't enough it truncates the oldest content. You can also use /export with the same behavior but it accepts arguments. One caveat: on remote machines the clipboard size limit means very long chats get trimmed or older parts dropped to fit.

how:07ee8f65525a:fd09d9628ab5:e5b398f323.q: What does the /dashboard command do, and how do I use it?
how:07ee8f65525a:fd09d9628ab5:e5b398f323.answer: The /dashboard command opens your Freebuff account hub in a web browser, showing your usage, daily streak, activity, tokens, and session history across the CLI, Desktop, and web. Typing /dashboard (or its aliases /usage, /stats, /streak) prints the URL to the chat and then attempts to open it via safeOpen, which prints the address as a fallback on headless Linux or locked-down WSL where no browser can launch automatically. In Codebuff this command is hidden, because Codebuff retains its own credits-based /usage banner; the dashboard aliases only apply to Freebuff builds. So in Freebuff you will get a system message with the account URL and your default browser opening, while Codebuff keeps its existing usage display and no-op redirect.

how:0ad116999e20:fd09d9628ab5:24b0b8eb04.q: What does the /diagnostics command do, and how do I use it?
how:0ad116999e20:fd09d9628ab5:24b0b8eb04.answer: The /diagnostics command prints a health report showing the app's CLI resource usage and the process IDs of any active terminal tools. It is registered in cli/src/commands/command-registry.ts as a command with aliases 'diag' and 'processes'. When invoked, it calls collectProcessDiagnostics (cli/src/commands/process-diagnostics.ts), which gathers version, runtime, platform, uptime, CPU time, memory usage, the parent and CLI PIDs, terminal watchdog state, and the list of active terminal command processes obtained via getActiveTerminalCommandProcesses from the SDK. The output is formatted by formatProcessDiagnostics and posted into the chat as a system message, and it deliberately omits command lines and environment variables so the report is safe to paste into a bug report. Active terminal tool process IDs are included so users can identify stray processes, while the watchdog status shows whether an external terminal watchdog is armed. The command is not Freebuff-only and is available in both Codebuff and Freebuff builds.

how:b970fc2828b0:fd09d9628ab5:247c2de63e.q: What does the /export command do, and how do I use it?
how:b970fc2828b0:fd09d9628ab5:247c2de63e.answer: The `/export` command saves the full conversation to a file in the project root. By default it writes Markdown (same rendering as `/copy`), or raw JSON if the filename ends in `.json`. Usage: - `/export` — writes to `codebuff-chat-<chatId>.md` (or `freebuff-chat-<chatId>.md` in Freebuff) - `/export my-notes.md` — writes Markdown to `my-notes.md` - `/export transcript.json` — writes raw message objects as JSON It resolves the filename relative to the project root and refuses to write outside that root or overwrite an existing file. It uses the persistence-safe `serializeForPersistence` serializer so cyclic tool output cannot throw, and writes asynchronously to avoid blocking the render thread. Note: `export` is no longer an alias for `/copy`; `/copy` now uses only `copy-chat`. Use `/export` to save to a file and `/copy` to copy to the clipboard. Caveat: a multi-MB transcript can throw during serialization (e.g. RangeError: Invalid string length), which surfaces as an ExportResult error rather than an unhandled rejection.

how:e054d5c9ff01:fd09d9628ab5:a2e8c8975f.q: What does the /queue command do, and how do I use it?
how:e054d5c9ff01:fd09d9628ab5:a2e8c8975f.answer: The /queue command opens a full-screen panel for editing, reordering, or deleting queued messages while the assistant is still answering. Type /queue in the CLI chat (or press Ctrl+Q) to swap the normal typing area for a list view of pending messages. In the panel: up/down or k/j moves the selection, Shift+up/down or J/K moves a message in the queue, t moves the selected message to the top, e (or Enter) opens an editor to rewrite the message, d (or delete/backspace) deletes the selected message, and Escape (or Ctrl+Q or q) closes the panel. The panel closes automatically once the queue empties, and if a message you're editing starts running mid-edit, the panel will tell you instead of applying the change. There is no /q alias, because q already quits the CLI. The panel takes the composer's place while open, and the keyboard focus is handed back to the composer when it closes.

how:8a557ff94e0a:fd09d9628ab5:ffa8fd87aa.q: What changed here, and what do I need to do about it? (Auth accepts null name from login response)
how:8a557ff94e0a:fd09d9628ab5:ffa8fd87aa.answer: The change makes the CLI credentials parser accept a null `name` field from the login response instead of failing. Specifically, in `cli/src/utils/auth.ts`, the `userSchema` now uses `z.string().nullish().transform((name) => name ?? '')` for the `name` field rather than `z.string()`. This allows login responses where the server-side user record has a null name to parse successfully, so those users can stay logged in without the app crashing on startup. The `saveUserCredentials` function writes a normalized user object where `name` is set to `user.name ?? ''`, preserving the existing on-disk shape. Additionally, `cli/src/login/plain-login.ts` prints the success message using the email when the name is absent or empty. This unblocks Freebuff and Codebuff accounts whose server-side user record has a null name, since the server's `userSchema` in `common/src/util/credentials.ts` already permits null names and the login response is written to disk as-is. Previously, requiring a string name caused every launch to fail parsing the credentials file for these accounts.

how:3db9cceb276c:fd09d9628ab5:d3be5da654.q: What changed here, and what do I need to do about it? (Freebuff CLI adopts multi-session claim IDs and relaunch handoff)

If a session takeover ever happens, you will see a message telling you to restart Freebuff rather than an automatic switch. A crash or closed terminal no longer forces a second hour purchase — the CLI can now resume an unexpired hour left by a dead process on the same account. The changes are live today for Freebuff's free ad-funded CLI and apps; paid Codebuff subscriptions are unaffected.

how:e11a91ba58bb:fd09d9628ab5:38b7105970.q: What changed here, and what do I need to do about it? (Freebuff defers self-update install until the session exits)
how:e11a91ba58bb:fd09d9628ab5:38b7105970.answer: The Freebuff launcher now defers installing a downloaded self-update until the session exits, so an in-progress coding session is never interrupted by a binary replacement. The deferred binary is staged in a per-process temp directory and held in pendingUpdates; on exit attachExitHandler calls installPendingUpdate, which installs only if the staged version is newer than the on-disk copy. You do not need to do anything to trigger this; it is live for Freebuff users only. The change is driven by the createLauncher deferUpdatesUntilExit flag, so custom launcher integrators should set that flag if they want the same behavior, and historical wrapper paths still use immediate install.

how:cecad3bcb8bb:fd09d9628ab5:fa67625c41.q: How do I run Freebuff in CI or non-interactively?
how:cecad3bcb8bb:fd09d9628ab5:fa67625c41.answer: Run Freebuff interactively in a tmux session driven by scripts in scripts/tmux/ — these are the same helper scripts used for interactive CLI testing. Captures are auto-saved to debug/tmux-sessions/{session}/ for inspection. There is no headless/no-TTY flag exposed; the product is driven through tmux so the full interactive TUI path is exercised.

how:873615900272:fd09d9628ab5:a7aa518307.q: How do I give Freebuff a custom system prompt or instructions?
how:873615900272:fd09d9628ab5:a7aa518307.answer: You give Freebuff a custom system prompt or instructions by creating an override JSON file in your project's `.agents/templates/` directory. The file must match the agent type you want to customize and can append, prepend, or replace the system prompt, instructions prompt, or step prompt. For example, to extend the reviewer agent: 1. Create `.agents/templates/reviewer.json` in your project: ```json { "override": { "type": "CodebuffAI/reviewer", "version": "0.1.7", "systemPrompt": { "type": "append", "content": "Additional instructions: Focus on security vulnerabilities and performance issues." } } } ``` 2. The system detects `.agents/templates/*.json` and `.md` files automatically and applies overrides at runtime with no restart needed. Use `"type": "replace"` to swap the prompt entirely, `"prepend"` to add before the base, or `"append"` to add after. how:941d0dbf0299:fd09d9628ab5:d5b3d19be3.q: How do I use skills or custom agents?
how:941d0dbf0299:fd09d9628ab5:d5b3d19be3.answer: Both skills and custom agents are organized as files under an `.agents/` directory in your project (or `~/.agents/` for global ones) and are discovered automatically. For skills, create `.agents/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter (name, description, license, metadata) — the name must be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens and must match the directory name; the CLI loads these on demand via the `/skill:<name>` command, and the agent can also call the `skill` tool to pull in a skill's full instructions. Project-level definitions in `.agents/skills/` and `.agents/` override global ones in `~/.agents/`. The `loadLocalAgents` and `loadSkills`/`loadSkillsSync` helpers in the SDK power this discovery, and agent files can be `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs` (test and `.d.ts` files are skipped).

how:b6b3f98fedf7:fd09d9628ab5:c807954462.q: How do I search this site for a change?
how:b6b3f98fedf7:fd09d9628ab5:c807954462.answer: Yes, this site has a search page. To search it: 1. **Go to `/search`** — that's the search page with a query box at the top. 2. **Type your question** — plain words work like they always did (e.g. `muse`, `claude`, `CLI`). 3. **Use field syntax** for more control: - `cat:cli` — filter by category - `sig:>=notable` — filter by impact (major/notable/minor) - `aud:end-users` — filter by audience - `"exact phrase"` — match a phrase - `-word` — exclude a word - `is:release`, `is:breaking`, `is:security`, `is:model`, etc. — filter by flag 4. **Quick chips** — click the preset filters above the box (e.g. `--models`, `--major`, `--cli`) for common searches. 5. **The URL updates** as you search, so you can bookmark or share any result view. Search covers entry titles, plain-English lines, categories, file paths, technical summaries, and evidence citations. You can also press `/` from anywhere on the site to jump straight to the search box. If you need something more specific, let me know what you're looking for and I can help craft the right query.

how:33a0cfda3eb8:fd09d9628ab5:e4bf35e1f2.q: How do I see the changes for a specific date range?

how:97f90f7c1cc0:fd09d9628ab5:c807954462.q: What do the significance badges like notable and major mean?
how:97f90f7c1cc0:fd09d9628ab5:c807954462.answer: The significance badges classify how much a change matters. `[MAJOR]` marks model catalog changes and version bumps that also ship code; `[NOTABLE]` marks user-visible feature work; minor/internal changes carry no badge. `[SECURITY]` flags trust, checksum, credential, privacy, or sandboxing changes. `[BREAKING]` means existing behavior, config, an API, or a command changed. `[LOW CONFIDENCE]` means the summary was truncated or a motive was guessed. `[MODEL]` marks catalog moves, and `[EDITED]` marks a human-corrected row. Badges link to the complete `/changes/<slice>/` page. The deterministic rule says one thing; the AI-weighted value (if it overrides the rule) is shown in the badge tooltip.

how:2c78a7f9061a:fd09d9628ab5:504ab3f453.q: What does the stale indicator mean, and why is it showing?
how:2c78a7f9061a:fd09d9628ab5:504ab3f453.answer: The [stale Nm] badge means the changelog data has not been re-analyzed from the upstream Freebuff repository within the site's freshness budget. It is derived from `changelog.generatedAt`, which only the analyze pass updates. The badge turns stale past 2x the `CHANGELOG_SYNC_STALE_MIN` budget (default 5 minutes, so 10 minutes), measured in raw milliseconds rather than floored minutes. It shows when the self-perpetuating sync relay in `.github/workflows/changelog-sync.yml` has fallen behind -- either because the loop is not running, a cycle is in flight, or failures have stretched over the freshness budget. The CI gate `cli.mjs freshness` fails the deploy if `data/changelog.json` is older than the badge would call stale, so a green site build means the badge will not be showing.

how:73d9b673aaa0:fd09d9628ab5:1518864732.q: Is there an API I can query this data from?
how:73d9b673aaa0:fd09d9628ab5:1518864732.answer: Yes. Freebuff has a read-only API that serves the same data as the static pages. Endpoints include /api/entry/<sha>.json (one entry's record: title, summary, plainEnglish, significance, audience, files, stats, release, links), /api/entries.json (newest 60 full records), /api/days.json (day index), /api/status.json (build stamp + head sha + counts + freshness), /api/traffic.json (14-day clone counts), /api/sha-day.json (sha to day lookup), and /api/records/<day>.json (per-day record shards). All JSON endpoints are CORS-open (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * in _headers). One non-API route is also dynamic: /release/<v>/?format=md returns release notes as text/markdown.

how:c695ae0353a3:fd09d9628ab5:508ef305e5.q: How do I see which changes came from which pull request?
how:c695ae0353a3:fd09d9628ab5:508ef305e5.answer: Each entry card shows where it came from. Upstream snapshot commits carry no PR number in their message, so the tool recovers the related PR by matching the set of files the snapshot touched against the file lists it has seen for open and recently merged PRs. A matched PR is shown on the card with a link to the pull request and a confidence marker ("likely, not certain" for file-set matches, exact for number or commit-SHA matches). You can also browse open pull requests on `/in-flight/`, where each card carries an AI preview written from the PR description and its stored diff. If a card shows no PR, the recovery found no file-set match within 14 days of the commit.

how:54713d5627a2:fd09d9628ab5:673295cc45.q: How often is this site updated, and how far behind is it?
how:54713d5627a2:fd09d9628ab5:673295cc45.answer: The site updates continuously: a sync relay polls upstream Freebuff every 30s in ~12-minute cycles, pushing new data every few minutes, and the static site is rebuilt and deployed on each data update. A scheduled deploy runs as a backstop. The site reports its own freshness in the footer badge and `/api/status.json`, measured against a 5-minute staleness budget (the site is flagged stale past 2x that, i.e. 10 minutes). So in normal operation the site is essentially live with upstream, not batched hourly or daily. You can see the current lag on the homepage footer or `/api/status.json`; a value in the single-digit minutes means it's running on time. The limit is the continuous relay itself: if that loop dies, the badge turns amber/stale and a CI freshness gate fails the deploy rather than shipping frozen data.

how:e088e7fe6e77:fd09d9628ab5:c807954462.q: What is the difference between this site and the official changelog?
how:e088e7fe6e77:fd09d9628ab5:c807954462.answer: This site is an **unofficial** changelog that reconstructs what actually shipped in Freebuff from the git diffs behind upstream's opaque snapshot commits; the official changelog is whatever Freebuff itself publishes (if anything). The reconstructed entries here are generated by diffing each public commit, classifying changes by area and significance, and optionally enriching them with AI-written technical summaries and plain-English ELI5 lines that cite the diff as evidence. It is built from the raw commit history of CodebuffAI/freebuff, not from any release notes document, so it is a third-party mirror and analysis, not the product's own changelog. The difference is the source of truth: this site's is the git diff; the official changelog's would be whatever release notes Freebuff chooses to ship.

how:0ad116999e20:fd09d9628ab5:415da246ae.q: What does the /diagnostics command do, and how do I use it?
how:0ad116999e20:fd09d9628ab5:415da246ae.answer: The `/diagnostics` command prints a health report showing how the CLI is using your computer's resources and which terminal tasks are currently running. You type it in chat as `/diagnostics` (or the aliases `/diag` or `/processes`). It shows the product name (Freebuff or Codebuff), the CLI version, the runtime and platform, how long the app has been open, CPU time in seconds, memory usage (RSS and heap used in human-readable units), the parent and CLI process IDs, the terminal watchdog status, and the process IDs of any in-flight terminal tools (with process group IDs on POSIX). Process group IDs are shown only on POSIX systems. Command lines and environment variables are deliberately omitted so the report is safe to paste into a bug report. The output appears as a system message in the chat.

how:b970fc2828b0:fd09d9628ab5:c950c06e9b.q: What does the /export command do, and how do I use it?
how:b970fc2828b0:fd09d9628ab5:c950c06e9b.answer: The `/export [filename]` command saves the current chat conversation to a file in the project root. By default it writes Markdown (the same rendering as `/copy`, via serializeConversation) into `freebuff-chat-<chatId>.md` (or `codebuff-chat-<chatId>.md` on Codebuff). Appending `.json` to the filename switches to raw JSON output, serialized with the persistence-safe serializer so cyclic tool output cannot throw. The file is created with an atomic write and is never overwritten — if the target file already exists the command returns an error asking for a new filename — and the resolved path must remain inside the project root. The command is registered in the CLI command registry and appears in the `/help` banner.

how:ba0e796a93ff:fd09d9628ab5:2243058771.q: What changed here, and what do I need to do about it? (Clipboard copy on Linux appends fix-it hint when only OSC 52 worked)
how:ba0e796a93ff:fd09d9628ab5:2243058771.answer: The latest change (commit e27f00b1, dated 2026-09-26) modified copyTextToClipboard in cli/src/utils/clipboard.ts. On Linux, when a local session falls back to OSC 52 because no native platform clipboard tool (wl-copy/xclip/xsel) succeeds, the app now appends a LINUX_OSC52_ONLY_HINT to the usual 'Copied' toast and extends the toast duration to 6000ms. This tells the user the copy went through the terminal (OSC 52) rather than a real clipboard, and suggests installing wl-clipboard or xclip if pasting fails. Native-tool copies on Linux still show the unchanged plain message, and this only triggers when no native tool was available. To act: if you see this hint, install a clipboard tool (e.g. sudo apt install wl-clipboard or sudo apt install xclip) for reliable clipboard access, or use Shift+drag in terminals that block OSC 52.

how:e11a91ba58bb:fd09d9628ab5:7f2092d694.q: What changed here, and what do I need to do about it? (Freebuff defers self-update install until the session exits)
how:e11a91ba58bb:fd09d9628ab5:7f2092d694.answer: Freebuff now defers installing any downloaded self-update until you close the CLI session, so your in-progress session is never replaced or interrupted by a new binary. No action is needed from you — the update downloads silently in the background and completes the moment you exit; you'll get the new version the next time you open Freebuff. A second launcher invocation will not replace or delete a staged binary while yours is still running, and an update restart hands the held session hour off to the new process. If a download loses the race with exit, it does not install into the running process's files. This behavior is live today for Freebuff users only (not Codebuff). You will not see downloads or installations happening mid-session.

how:f7a686c23ed2:fd09d9628ab5:f82af14e80.answer: Solar Pro 4 is now capped at 1 session per day in the Freebuff free tier. The model is also pinned to the tag-qualified OpenRouter endpoint `upstage/zdr` (later `upstage`) rather than the bare provider slug. If you hit the cap, Freebuff refuses the session and names the model as an experimental trial via `freebuffSessionSpendNotice`; switching to another model (e.g. GLM 5.3 Flash or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which are unmetered at full access) lets you continue immediately. The change is explicitly a measurement window: read the cache rate and $/msg on /web/admin/spend after the pin has been live a full day, and if they land near other premium rows, raise or remove the cap so the shared premium pool meters the row alone. No client action is required, and the notice is shown before you start a session.

how:1566e32f271b:fd09d9628ab5:8ee073a05e.answer: Freebuff now **hard-blocks** VPN, proxy, and Tor traffic in free mode instead of downgrading it to limited mode. If you use a VPN, proxy, or Tor, Freebuff will refuse to run entirely and show a message (e.g. 'Freebuff cannot be used from VPN, proxy, or Tor traffic. Please disable it and try again.'). To use Freebuff again, turn off the VPN/proxy/Tor, then restart Freebuff. The CLI surfaces this as a 403 country_blocked response in the waiting-room screen with a VPN/proxy/Tor-specific message. Residential proxies and Tor remain hard-blocked; hosting, relay, anonymous, and service signals remain limited rather than hard-blocked.

how:664df805be46:fd09d9628ab5:73cdb5ebf8.answer: The `--save-traces` flag is a CLI option for the BuffBench evaluation framework that, when passed to the main entrypoint scripts (`main.ts`, `main-nightly.ts`, `main-hard-tasks.ts`, `main-single-eval.ts`), enables writing agent execution traces to disk. Specifically, when the flag is present, the `saveTraces` boolean is parsed via `process.argv.includes('--save-traces')` and forwarded to `runBuffBench`, which in turn passes it down to `runTask`. Inside `runTask`, when `saveTraces` is true, each agent's full trace (the raw `agentResult.trace` array of `AgentStep` objects) is written as a JSON file into a `logsDir/traces` subdirectory, with filenames like `{taskIndex}-{safeTaskId}-{safeAgentId}-{safeCommitShort}-agent.json`. The traces are persisted only when the flag is explicitly set — by default, no trace files are written, preserving the original behavior. This is intended for deep debugging of how coding agents behave during evaluation runs, allowing reviewers to inspect the exact sequence of tool calls, messages, and decisions each agent made.

how:8fc301cbf50a:fd09d9628ab5:73e9b5036e.q: What is the CODEBUFF_GITHUB_ACTIONS environment variable, what values does it take, and when do I need it?
how:8fc301cbf50a:fd09d9628ab5:73e9b5036e.answer: CODEBUFF_GITHUB_ACTIONS is an environment variable set to the string 'true' in GitHub Actions CI workflows to signal that the code is running in CI. When its value is 'true', local-only behaviors are disabled: file-based log transports are skipped, local test environment defaults/stubs are not applied, and DB-backed tests throw instead of running. It is read at runtime in several places (common/src/env.ts for IS_CI, common/src/env-ci.ts in the ciEnv snapshot, packages/internal/src/env.ts and common/src/env.ts to gate relaxed test defaults, backend/src/util/logger.ts and related loggers to skip file logging, sdk/src/byok.ts and backend loggers to skip splitAndLog/localFileTransport, and evals/buffbench/logger.ts to skip debug file logging). Set it to 'true' only in CI workflow job environment/overrides (e.g., .github/workflows freebuff-release.yml and ci.yml set it for npm-app/backend/common test jobs); otherwise leave it unset so local development keeps file logs and relaxed env defaults.

how:7719cbe68895:fd09d9628ab5:f7625639eb.q: What is the CODEBUFF_IS_BINARY environment variable, what values does it take, and when do I need it?
how:7719cbe68895:fd09d9628ab5:f7625639eb.answer: `CODEBUFF_IS_BINARY` is a compile-time flag injected into the CLI binary via `process.env.CODEBUFF_IS_BINARY='"true"'` in `defineFlags` (see `cli/scripts/build-binary.ts`). Its value is always the string `"true"` when the code runs inside a shipped binary, and it is `undefined` in dev mode. You need it (or it is needed for you) when distinguishing whether the binary is running as a compiled executable versus `bun run dev`; notably `cli/src/native/ripgrep.ts` uses `getCliEnv().CODEBUFF_IS_BINARY` to decide whether to self-extract the bundled ripgrep or fall back to the SDK path, and `cli/src/utils/terminal-command-broker.ts`'s `defaultBrokerInvocation` switches between the compiled binary's `--terminal-command-broker` flag and a source `entry.ts` invocation based on it. For Freebuff, note `FREEBUFF_MODE` is the analogous flag for that variant, not `CODEBUFF_IS_BINARY`.

how:55c6ff3a72ed:fd09d9628ab5:096498fa3b.answer: CODEBUFF_TRACE is an environment variable that, when set to 1 (or true/yes), turns on detailed execution traces written to trace.jsonl inside each chat directory. It is one of several CLI-specific env vars declared in cli/src/types/env.ts and read via getCliEnv(). In dev/test it stays off by default; in production builds tracing is always disabled unless you explicitly export CODEBUFF_TRACE=1 before launching the binary. You need it only if you want per-step agent message histories captured for debugging — set it for production debugging, leave it unset otherwise.

how:fac475c142f0:fd09d9628ab5:82bd386927.q: What is the FREEBUFF_CONFIG_DIR environment variable, what values does it take, and when do I need it?
how:fac475c142f0:fd09d9628ab5:82bd386927.answer: FREEBUFF_CONFIG_DIR is an environment variable that overrides the directory where the Freebuff CLI stores its config (credentials.json, settings.json, message-history.json, etc.). how:158662636fb4:fd09d9628ab5:485c0cd78a.q: What is the FREEBUFF_MODE environment variable, what values does it take, and when do I need it?
how:158662636fb4:fd09d9628ab5:485c0cd78a.answer: FREEBUFF_MODE is a compile-time environment variable (not a runtime setting you set yourself). It takes the value 'true' during the build to produce the Freebuff binary, and 'false' otherwise. The CLI reads it via process.env.FREEBUFF_MODE and exposes it as the IS_FREEBUFF constant in cli/src/utils/constants.ts; when that constant is true, the build is Freebuff and the code strips out paid features (subscribe, usage, ads toggling, mode switching) and rebrands as Freebuff. You never set FREEBUFF_MODE yourself at the shell: it is injected by bun build --define in cli/scripts/build-binary.ts (see the defineFlags array, which writes process.env.FREEBUFF_MODE="${process.env.FREEBUFF_MODE ?? 'false'}"), and freebuff/cli/build.ts sets it to 'true' before invoking that build script for the Freebuff release. A non-free mode build simply leaves it unset/false, so the regular Codebuff binary is produced instead.

how:ad5f68d47284:fd09d9628ab5:acfde04633.q: What is the VERBOSE environment variable, what values does it take, and when do I need it?
how:ad5f68d47284:fd09d9628ab5:acfde04633.answer: VERBOSE is an environment variable that controls verbose/debug output. It is read as a string in process.env and is considered "true" only when set to the exact value 'true' (other values, including unset, mean verbose mode is off). Set VERBOSE=true when you need to debug the CLI build (build-binary.ts uses it to switch command stdio from 'pipe' to 'inherit' and print log lines) or when you need verbose credit consumption and Stripe sync debug logs in the backend's message-cost-tracker.ts. In normal operation it is left unset/false so output stays clean.

how:800a5a0bab8a:fd09d9628ab5:0effd7776a.q: What is the ZED_SHELL environment variable, what values does it take, and when do I need it?
how:800a5a0bab8a:fd09d9628ab5:0effd7776a.answer: ZED_SHELL is a CLI-specific environment variable used for Zed editor terminal detection, surfaced in cli/src/utils/env.ts via getCliEnv() and typed as an optional string in cli/src/types/env.ts. It does not require a specific value; when Codebuff launches from within the Zed editor it inspect't set, the CLI inspects SHELL, TERM_PROGRAM, VSCODE_*, CURSOR, JETBRAINS_*, and related fields to identify the enclosing terminal/IDE, and ZED_TERM/ZED_NODE_ENV/ZED_SHELL are read only as passive detection hints (no Zed-specific code path depends on a particular ZED_SHELL value). You do not need to set ZED_SHELL yourself unless you are debugging terminal detection; the variable is consumed implicitly during shell detection (see detectShell in cli/src/utils/detect-shell.ts using env.SHELL/COMSPEC with platform-specific fallbacks) and there is no public documentation specifying the values Zed assigns to it. Coverage note: the provided material defines ZED_SHELL as a detected field but does not document the exact values Zed sets nor any case where you must provide it manually.
